title: what the Rig Veda is
hook: a night-shift nurse walks out into a sky going pink. The Rig Veda sings to that light by name: Ushas, the dawn

segments.voice: Yesterday, what the Rig Veda is: Vasishtha asking Varuna, what did I do, and naming drink, anger and dice. Did you ask someone what happened, instead of guessing? Day one thousand two hundred forty-eight.

The hospital doors slide open and a nurse steps out after a long night shift. Her feet hurt. Her head is full of beeping. And then she looks up. The sky over the parking lot is going from gray to rose to gold, and for a second she forgets everything else. The birds have started. A bus hisses at the corner. The whole street is waking up, and she's watching it happen, as if it were being done for her. Plenty of mornings like this go by unseen. The Rig Veda's poets didn't. They turned to that light, gave it a name, and sang to it. Today, Ushas, the dawn.
screen: `OUT OF THE NIGHT SHIFT.` → `GRAY, ROSE, GOLD.` → `THE POETS SANG TO IT.`

segments.voice: Ushas is the dawn, and in the Rig Veda she's a goddess, pictured as a young woman in bright clothes, driving away the dark. One hymn to her begins, in paraphrase: this light has come, the fairest of lights. Her bright sign is born. Then the poet notices something about time. The night, he says, has made room for the dawn, like a sister giving way to her sister. And then this line. Gone are the mortals who watched the earlier dawns. Now she is seen by us. And coming are those who will see her in mornings still ahead. Three groups of people, under one light: those before us, us, and those after. Every sunrise, on this reading, joins them. The same hymn ends by waking everyone up. Rise, it says. The breath of life has come back to us. The dark has gone away. Light is coming near. She has opened a path for the sun to travel. The hymn holds two things together: one life is short, and the light it's lived under is shared. And the dawn isn't new each day. She is ancient and young at once, the hymn says, coming again and again.
screen: `USHAS: THE DAWN, A GODDESS.` · `THE FAIREST OF LIGHTS HAS COME.` · `THOSE BEFORE, US, THOSE AFTER.` · `RISE: THE BREATH HAS COME BACK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: greet the light. If you can, turn toward a window, or step outside. If it's night, call a dawn you remember to mind. Sit, and let the breath come and go. Feel the light on your face, real or remembered. Then let three groups come to mind: someone before you who saw this sky and is gone. Someone with you now. Someone who will see it after you. Hold all three in the same light for a while. If you pray, you can greet the morning in your own way. The bell holds the time.
What the Rig Veda is. Hymns that sing to Ushas, the dawn, fairest of lights, seen by those before us, by us, and by those still to come. Today's word.
screen: `WHAT THE RIG VEDA IS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: what the Rig Veda is. Tomorrow morning, catch the first light, even for ten seconds through a window, before you look at a screen. Day one thousand two hundred forty-eight.

screen: `DAY 1248 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT THE RIG VEDA IS.`

howItsDone: In Hindu practice, dawn is often a time of prayer: bathing, chanting, and offering water to the rising sun, and the hymns to Ushas are part of the Rig Veda's recited text.

fork.setup: you're the poet, watching the dawn. you think of the people who watched it before you, now gone. where does your hymn go next?
options: to us, and to those who'll see dawns still ahead.
fork.reveal: the hymn moves on: now she is seen by us, and coming are those who will see her later. one light joins them all.

original.note: Sanskrit: dawn, and the goddess of the dawn in the Rig Veda.

trapdoor: what you thought: Ushas is just the Sanskrit word for sunrise.
what it means: she's a goddess the poets sang to, the light that joins those before us, us, and those after.
what a scholar hears: Rig Veda 1.113, the hymn to Ushas by Kutsa, with its sisters night and dawn, and the mortals who saw the earlier dawns.
recall: stilling the movements of the mind
the year just walked and kept

sources.ref: Rig Veda 1.113.1–3 (this light has come, fairest of lights; night has yielded to dawn, sister to sister)
Rig Veda 1.113.11 (gone are the mortals who saw the earlier dawn; now she is seen by us; coming are those who will see her later)
Rig Veda 1.113.13, 1.113.16 (ancient and ever young; rise, the breath of life has come to us, darkness has gone, light approaches, she has opened a path for the sun)

notes: Rig Veda 1.113 paraphrased throughout (no PD translation on the validator list). Confirm verse numbers, especially 1.113.13 (ancient, ever young) and 1.113.16 (rise, the breath of life).
'The fairest of lights' is the hymn's own superlative (1.113.1).
Ushas pictured as a young woman in bright clothes is a standard summary of her hymns, not a quotation. Confirm.
Kutsa as the seer of 1.113 (trapdoor) is from the tradition's index; confirm.
howItsDone mentions offering water to the rising sun (arghya, often with the Gayatri); confirm.
